semantic_correction.stem: Which nursing focus is most consistent with end-of-life comfort care for a dying client?

options.A: Concentrate on physical symptoms and reduce conversation or family involvement so the client has fewer sources of stimulation during the dying process.
options.B: Follow the care team's preferred plan when it differs from the client's expressed wishes, because professional judgment should guide end-of-life priorities.
options.C: Continue burdensome disease-directed interventions whenever they remain technically available, even when they do not match the client's comfort-focused goals.
options.D: Relieve pain and other distressing symptoms while supporting emotional, spiritual, practical, and family needs in ways that reflect the client's wishes and goals.

semantic_correction.rationale: D is correct. Current National Institute on Aging guidance describes end-of-life care as support and medical care surrounding death that should reflect the person's preferences, needs, choices, and end-of-life wishes. NIA identifies four broad areas of need for people who are dying: physical comfort, mental and emotional needs, spiritual needs, and practical tasks; family members also need support. NIA guidance further emphasizes relieving pain and other discomfort and involving the dying person in decisions when possible. Hospice guidance similarly focuses on comfort, quality of life, symptom relief, and emotional and spiritual support for the person and family. Therefore the nursing focus should be multidimensional comfort care aligned with the client's goals and wishes. A is incorrect because emotional connection and family support may be important and should not be routinely withdrawn. B is incorrect because the client's preferences and advance-care wishes should guide care to the extent possible. C is incorrect because treatment that is burdensome or inconsistent with the client's comfort-focused goals should not be continued merely because it is technically available.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Prioritize multidimensional end-of-life comfort by relieving distressing symptoms and supporting emotional, spiritual, practical, and family needs according to the client's wishes and goals.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the absolute-word and answer-length cues, rebuilt all four end-of-life care approaches to comparable length and specificity, freshly verified current NIA end-of-life and hospice guidance, and preserved multidimensional comfort aligned with client wishes as the single best response.

audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort — end-of-life care and comfort measures
audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests multidimensional end-of-life comfort care with one clearly best response, balanced alternatives, current authoritative guidance, and no absolute-word or answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Incorrect. End-of-life care includes emotional, spiritual, practical, and family support in addition to physical symptom management.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Client preferences and end-of-life wishes should guide care to the extent possible rather than being displaced by team preference.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Comfort-focused goals should guide whether interventions remain appropriate; technical availability alone is not a reason to continue burdensome treatment.
option_audit.D: Correct. It directly reflects NIA's multidimensional comfort framework and alignment with the person's wishes and goals.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. D uniquely combines symptom relief, emotional/spiritual/practical/family support, and client-goal alignment; A narrows care, B overrides preferences, and C prioritizes treatment availability over comfort goals.
cueing_check: All four options are parallel end-of-life nursing approaches of comparable length and specificity; the prior absolute-word distractor and uniquely-long correct response were removed.
